title: Anoxic Bottom Waters of Lakes are Global Hotspots of Methane and Carbon Dioxide Accumulation
content:
Abstract

Lakes, ponds, and reservoirs (hereafter “lakes”) are substantial sources of the greenhouse gases (GHGs) carbon dioxide (CO2) and methane (CH4) to the Earth's atmosphere. The exchange of CO2 and CH4 between the lake surface and the atmosphere can be modulated by processes throughout the water column, including fixation, respiration, methanogenesis, and methanotrophy. However, insufficient characterization of GHG concentrations and drivers in the lower water column (bottom waters) has limited the incorporation of bottom-water biogeochemistry into emission models. Here, we analyzed depth profiles of dissolved CO2 and CH4 in 522 lakes across 38 countries and seven continents to examine the drivers of gas concentrations. Aggregated across lakes and sampling dates, both surface and bottom waters were commonly supersaturated in CO2 and CH4 relative to atmospheric equilibrium (surface median = 300% for CO2 and 14,000% for CH4). Median bottom-water concentrations were four times higher than surface concentrations for CO2 and 70 times higher for CH4. The highest surface-water concentrations of both gases were observed when bottom-water concentrations were also high. Dissolved oxygen (DO) was the primary covariate for bottom-water CO2 and CH4 among lakes, with high concentrations under low oxygen conditions (n = 121 lakes for CH4 and 147 for CO2). CO2 and CH4 concentrations were additionally associated with lake morphometry and trophic state, with the highest concentrations in small, nutrient-rich lakes. As climate change and eutrophication drive deoxygenation of lakes worldwide, our results highlight the potential for increased GHG concentrations under global change, which could in turn alter the future magnitude and timing of emissions.
